name: Tacrolimus ointment

lead: Tacrolimus ointment is a topical immunosuppressant sold as Protopic. It is prescribed for atopic dermatitis (eczema) and has been used for facial vitiligo, particularly in children.

It helps skin appearance by calming inflamed, red, itchy patches without thinning the skin as steroids can, and in vitiligo it is used to encourage return of pigment. Dermatology guidelines in Japan and elsewhere include it in eczema care.

paras: It is applied to affected skin under prescriber direction, commonly on face and eyelids where steroids are less suitable. Treatment is for active lesions or as maintenance as directed by a clinician.

Burning or itching early on and sun sensitivity are common effects [1]. In March 2005 the FDA issued a health warning on possible cancer risk based on animal and small patient data; a 2023 meta-analysis found no increased cancer risk with moderate certainty [1]. Prescription only.

angle.text: Used under medical direction, it treats visible patches of eczema and, in some people, facial vitiligo.

lead: Tacrolimus ointment, sold as Protopic (LEO Pharma), is a prescription topical calcineurin inhibitor used on visible inflammatory skin conditions, chiefly atopic dermatitis (eczema) and, in some patients, vitiligo.[1][2][3] Tacrolimus is a macrolide immunosuppressant first discovered in 1987 by a Japanese team led by Tohru Kino in the soil bacterium Streptomyces tsukubaensis; its name is derived from Tsukuba macrolide immunosuppressant.[1]

It matters for looks because eczema on the face and eyelids and patchy depigmentation from vitiligo are conspicuous. Wikipedia describes the ointment as about as effective as a mid-potency topical steroid without causing skin thinning, which is why it is used on thin-skinned areas such as the face; it is also used for segmental vitiligo in children, particularly on the face.[1] Atopic dermatitis often affects the cheeks and eyelids, and inflammation can leave patches lighter or darker than the surrounding skin that fade over months once the eczema is controlled.[2]

Research includes early trials of the ointment in atopic dermatitis, Japanese and other national guidelines that list it among first-line topical anti-inflammatory drugs, and a trial in alopecia areata that did not show regrowth.[4][5][6][7] Safety discussion centres on a 2005 FDA health warning about possible cancer risk, later large-scale analyses, and sun precautions.[1][8]
infobox: 1987, by a team led by Tohru Kino, from Streptomyces tsukubaensis[1]
Facial and eyelid eczema; segmental vitiligo (especially children)[1][2]

paras: Topical tacrolimus is prescribed for inflammatory and pigment-related skin conditions where appearance is affected, most often on the face.[1][2][3]

Atopic dermatitis is the main use. Wikipedia lists tacrolimus and pimecrolimus as the calcineurin inhibitors used in the condition and describes them as effective and safe, recommended in some places as first-line therapy and in others for when corticosteroids and moisturisers have not been sufficient.[2][1] The 2024 Japanese clinical practice guidelines name tacrolimus ointment among topical anti-inflammatory drugs, with topical corticosteroids, delgocitinib and difamilast ointments, used to induce remission quickly by suppressing skin inflammation and itch; refractory moderate-to-severe disease is addressed with oral cyclosporine, biologics, JAK inhibitors or phototherapy in addition to topical care.[5][6]

Facial involvement is common in atopic dermatitis: cheeks in infants and children, and eyelid swelling that can produce a prominent crease under the eye (Dennie-Morgan folds).[2] Because tacrolimus does not cause skin thinning, it is used on the face.[1]

Wikipedia's vitiligo article lists topical calcineurin inhibitors such as tacrolimus and pimecrolimus among first-line treatments alongside topical steroids, and reports that calcineurin inhibitors combined with phototherapy outperformed phototherapy alone.[3] Facial lesions respond most easily, probably because facial skin is thin, while hands, feet and joints are the hardest to repigment.[3] Ruxolitinib cream was approved in the United States in July 2022 as another topical option.[3] The tacrolimus article describes use for segmental vitiligo in children, especially on the face.[1]
The appearance impact of vitiligo is documented: Wikipedia notes the changed look can affect emotional wellbeing and employment, particularly when the face, hands or arms are involved.[3]

A 2001 review of tacrolimus in dermatology reported that short-term trials of the ointment in atopic dermatitis showed excellent results in adults and children, small studies in acute contact dermatitis, and animal findings that topical tacrolimus induces the anagen (growth) phase of hair and protects from chemotherapy-induced alopecia, while oral tacrolimus has been tried in psoriasis.[9] A 2005 open trial in 11 patients with alopecia areata covering 10 to 75 percent of the scalp used 0.1 percent tacrolimus ointment twice daily for 24 weeks and found no terminal hair growth; the authors suggested the ointment's limited penetration depth and patient selection might explain this.[7]

Tacrolimus binds the protein FKBP12, and the complex inhibits calcineurin. This blocks activation of the transcription factor NF-AT, reducing production of interleukin-2 and related cytokines and so suppressing T-cell activation and proliferation.[1] A 2001 review describes inhibition of IL-2, IL-3, IL-4, TNF-alpha and GM-CSF.[9] Pimecrolimus works through the same target; Wikipedia says unlike topical steroids neither causes skin atrophy.[8]

Wikipedia states that topical application results in little to no systemic bioavailability, in contrast to oral tacrolimus, which is metabolised mainly by CYP3A in the liver and gut and used in transplant medicine.[1]

Reported topical effects include burning or itching on application at first and increased sensitivity to sunlight and heat; less common ones include flu-like symptoms, headache, cough and burning eyes.[1] Precautions listed on Wikipedia include avoiding occlusive dressings, known or suspected malignant skin lesions, Netherton syndrome and certain skin infections, and limiting sun and UV exposure; pregnancy is listed as a precaution, with Australian pregnancy category C.[1]

The topical drug is a different exposure from oral tacrolimus, whose systemic side effects include infection, kidney toxicity and, in transplant recipients, increased lymphoma and skin cancer risk related to intensity and duration of immunosuppression.[1]

In March 2005 the FDA issued a health warning for tacrolimus and pimecrolimus based on animal models and a small number of patients; Wikipedia states UK dermatologists did not consider this a significant concern and increasingly recommended the drugs.[1] Wikipedia's pimecrolimus article records that in January 2006 the FDA required a boxed warning for potential lymphoma or skin cancer risk, that dermatology and allergy societies objected, and that an American Academy of Dermatology task force found no causal proof linking topical immunomodulators to lymphoma or non-melanoma skin cancer.[8]

A January 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis in The Lancet Child & Adolescent Health found, with moderate-certainty evidence, no increased cancer risk with the two topical drugs, and Wikipedia notes experts still debate appropriate indications and duration.[1][8] Separately, on 29 November 2024 the International Agency for Research on Cancer classified tacrolimus as a Group 1 carcinogen, a listing reported by Wikipedia without specifying the route of exposure considered.[1]

Tacrolimus was discovered in 1987 by a team led by Tohru Kino; Thomas Starzl's 1992 memoir gives a first-hand account of its early development in transplantation.[1] The FDA first approved it in 1994 for liver transplantation, and the EU approved the ointment for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis in 2002.[1] A 1994 Lancet letter reported tacrolimus ointment in atopic dermatitis, an early publication on the topical use.[4] A 2003 paper reviewed atopic dermatitis management with the ointment under the Protopic name.[10]

The class later grew with pimecrolimus (Elidel), which Novartis filed in December 2000 and the FDA approved on 13 December 2001.[8] Tacrolimus is on the WHO Essential Medicines List, and Protopic is marketed by LEO Pharma.[1]

Atopic dermatitis evidence rests on trials and guidelines: the Lancet 1994 letter and 2001 and 2003 papers describe early results, and the 2024 Japanese guidelines place tacrolimus ointment among current topical options.[4][9][10][5][6]

In vitiligo, Wikipedia reports calcineurin inhibitors as first-line, better with phototherapy, and most effective on the face.[3] A study published in Pediatric Research in 2023 examined metabolism in infants with vitiligo exposed to topical calcineurin inhibitors.[11] In alopecia areata, a 2005 open trial of 11 patients found no terminal hair growth.[7]
A January 2023 Lancet Child & Adolescent Health meta-analysis addressed cancer risk with topical calcineurin inhibitors and reported no increase with moderate certainty.[1][8]

Tacrolimus ointment is discussed mainly in dermatology rather than in looksmaxxing forums. In appearance contexts it comes up for eczema flares around the eyes and face and for vitiligo patches, usually as a prescription alternative when steroid thinning is a concern.[1][2] It is prescription-only in the United States, Canada and the EU.[1]

claims.claim: It calms facial eczema without the skin thinning seen with steroids
It can bring pigment back in vitiligo
The ointment regrows hair in alopecia areata
Little of it enters the bloodstream when applied to skin

timeline.event: Tacrolimus discovered by a team led by Tohru Kino.[1]
US approval (initially liver transplantation); Lancet letter on tacrolimus ointment for atopic dermatitis.[1][4]
FDA approves pimecrolimus (Elidel) on 13 December; review of tacrolimus in dermatology published.[8][9]
EU approval of tacrolimus ointment for atopic dermatitis.[1]
FDA health warning on possible cancer risk (March); open trial in alopecia areata finds no terminal regrowth.[1][7]
FDA requires boxed warning for topical calcineurin inhibitors (January).[8]
Ruxolitinib cream approved in the US for vitiligo (July), adding a non-calcineurin topical option.[3]
Lancet Child & Adolescent Health meta-analysis finds no increased cancer risk with moderate certainty.[1][8]
IARC classifies tacrolimus as Group 1 (29 November); Japanese atopic dermatitis guidelines updated.[1][5]
